questions.q: What does CHAR(5) do when storing the value 'OK'?
options: Truncates it to 2 characters and shrinks the column
Stores only 'OK' using 2 characters of space, same as VARCHAR
Rejects the value with an error
Pads it with trailing spaces to store exactly 5 characters: 'OK   '
questions.explain: CHAR always allocates and stores the full declared length, padding shorter values with spaces.

questions.q: How does VARCHAR(50) store a 3-character name?
options: It rejects values shorter than 50 characters
Using roughly 3 characters of storage, not the full 50
It rounds up to the nearest 10 characters
Using exactly 50 characters, padded like CHAR
questions.explain: VARCHAR only uses the space actually needed for the stored value, up to its declared maximum.

questions.q: When should you prefer CHAR over VARCHAR?
options: CHAR should never be used in modern SQL Server
For values that are genuinely fixed-length in the real world, like country codes or state abbreviations
For all text columns, always
Only for numeric data
questions.explain: CHAR fits data with a truly consistent length; using it for variable-length text wastes space.

questions.q: What happens if a value exceeds a column's declared CHAR/VARCHAR length?
options: SQL Server converts the column to a different data type automatically
The value is truncated (or an error is raised, depending on settings) rather than the column silently growing
The column automatically resizes itself to fit the longer value
Nothing — there is no length enforcement at all
questions.explain: A declared length is a hard limit — oversized input causes truncation or an error, a common source of unexpected data loss.

questions.q: Why is VARCHAR the overwhelmingly common default for real-world text?
options: VARCHAR is required for any column that might contain a NULL
Most real text (names, addresses, descriptions) genuinely varies in length, and VARCHAR avoids wasting space on padding
VARCHAR is always faster than CHAR in every scenario
CHAR cannot store more than 10 characters
questions.explain: Using CHAR for variable-length data wastes storage and can introduce subtle trailing-space comparison bugs.
